report.headline: Usage rate projected to climb from 21.2% in the NBA to 25.0% in the EuroLeague, but the shooting-efficiency projection carries no signal.

projection.text: The model projects a usage rate of 25.0% in the EuroLeague, up from 21.2% in the 2007-08 NBA season, against a EuroLeague average of 20.6% (SD 4.4%) — roughly one standard deviation above the league mean.

risks.text: The true shooting projection of 58.4% should not be trusted: the model's out-of-fold error (4.7%) is no better than simply guessing the league-mean baseline (4.7%) for this metric.

Even for usage, the 80% interval (20.6%-29.4%) and 95% interval (18.3%-31.8%) span roughly two to three standard deviations of the EuroLeague distribution, so the projection is far better suited to ranking a cohort than pricing this individual.

Players who historically made this NBA-to-EuroLeague move sat on average 0.31 sd below their own league's average, while this subject sat 0.23 sd above it — a mismatch with the profile underlying the 115-transition estimate.
The evidence base is a single NBA season at age 28 (82 games, 2,117 minutes), leaving no multi-year track record to corroborate the projected role change.

strengths.text: The subject carried a usage rate 0.23 standard deviations above the NBA average across a full 82-game, 2,117-minute season, indicating an established high-usage role rather than a small sample.
Shot selection leaned heavily toward three-pointers (56.4% of attempts) while posting a source-season true shooting mark of 54.0%, essentially at the NBA league average (+0.02 sd).
Ball-handling was balanced for a high-usage wing: a 14.2% assist rate against a 13.9% turnover rate in the source season.
The usage projection model outperforms the trivial league-mean baseline (3.3% MAE vs 4.3%), so the projected rise in usage rests on a model shown to add value on this metric.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage rate runs from 20.6% to 29.4% — about two standard deviations of the EuroLeague usage distribution — and widens to 18.3%-31.8% at 95%. The model beats the trivial league-mean baseline on this metric (3.3% MAE vs 4.3%), so it can rank players but cannot pin an individual's role tightly.
